analysis.one_liner: Closes the "generally recognized as safe" loophole so food additives must be disclosed to and reviewed by the FDA before sale.
analysis.headline: The bill to require safety notification and public disclosure for food additives marketed as "generally recognized as safe" was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never advanced.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current rules, a company can decide on its own that a food chemical is "generally recognized as safe" (GRAS) and sell it in food without ever telling the FDA. This bill would order the FDA to rewrite its rules so that a company must notify the agency, submit safety evidence, and wait 90 days for public review before using a GRAS substance; it would also ban novel and cancer-causing chemicals from GRAS status, bar conflicted experts from the safety panels, and force a re-review of chemicals cleared under the old rules. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Health subcommittee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress expired.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, especially children and other vulnerable populations, would gain: food chemicals could no longer be self-certified as safe in secret. The FDA would get notification of every GRAS determination, the public would get 90 days to review and object to each one, and the full safety data would be posted online. People exposed to chemicals through multiple foods would be better protected because safety reviews would have to account for cumulative effects and impacts on developing bodies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, especially children and vulnerable groups

how_it_helps.text: It would prohibit selling food with a GRAS substance unless the manufacturer has notified the FDA and submitted supporting safety information, including the substance's cumulative effects and impacts on vulnerable populations.
It requires the FDA to post every GRAS determination and its supporting data on a public website, with at least 90 days for the agency and the public to review and object.
It bars newly synthesized or novel chemicals and carcinogenic substances from being deemed GRAS, and bars the FDA from relying on experts with conflicts of interest in GRAS determinations.
It would require systematic reassessment of substances previously determined GRAS under the looser standards, assisted by a reestablished Food Advisory Committee.

analysis.who_pays: Food manufacturers and ingredient suppliers would bear the cost of preparing safety submissions, disclosing their evidence publicly, and potentially losing the ability to sell some chemicals — including reassessing ones already in use. Some costs would likely pass to consumers through food prices.

drawbacks.text: Requiring companies to notify the FDA and disclose the basis for every GRAS determination would add compliance work and could slow the introduction of new food ingredients.

Systematically reopening past GRAS determinations and barring novel and carcinogenic substances could sweep in many chemicals at once, and opponents would argue the current voluntary notice system already lets FDA challenge unsafe substances.
The bill mandates rulemaking on fixed deadlines and reestablishes an advisory committee, adding regulatory machinery whose costs are not paid for in the bill text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — closing a loophole that lets companies add chemicals to food without independent safety review — are real, and the bill was deliberately written to be modest, targeting FDA rules rather than banning any ingredient. The costs are modest too: industry compliance and some delay in bringing new ingredients to market, plus a risk of the reassessment process creating backlogs. On balance, the cost side is small; the bigger cost of this bill's outcome was that it never got a hearing, so none of these tradeoffs were even litigated.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee, referred to a Health subcommittee, and the Congress ended without a markup or a vote.

narrative.text: Introduced June 4, 2021, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce three days later.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Health on June 7, 2021, and no further action appears in the record.
The bill received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no action in the Senate before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Food manufacturers and ingredient companies keep the current system in which they can market new chemicals as 'generally recognized as safe' without FDA notification, and the FDA's conflict-of-interest and disclosure rules remain unchanged.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and directed FDA rulemaking to close the GRAS self-certification loophole.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral without a markup, hearing, or vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Food industry groups
against.role: Trade associations representing food and beverage manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Historically opposed mandatory GRAS notification rules; no opposition activity appears in the congressional record for this bill.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; support was entirely Democratic (the sponsor and 9 Democratic cosponsors), and no Republican support or opposition appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill ends the practice of self-certifying new chemicals as GRAS without telling the FDA, and forces disclosure of safety data, reassessment of old determinations, and conflict-free expert panels. Ordinary people eating processed food gain a safety check; companies lose a cheap, secret pathway to market.
Suppliers of novel additives could no longer claim GRAS status for newly synthesized chemicals or carcinogens, and previously cleared substances could be reassessed and pulled from the market.

industries.industry: Food safety testing and toxicology consultants
industries.note: Mandatory safety submissions, cumulative-effect reviews, and systematic reassessments would create demand for independent toxicology work and conflict-free expert panels.
